investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
investigations.objective: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections. The primary variables include: Forced flow velocity (speed and direction) Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation) Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets
investigations.hypothesis: BASS-II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.
investigations.research_impacts: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you're on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.objective: The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
investigations.hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time - longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
investigations.research_impacts: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques. BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
investigations.objective: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
investigations.research_impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA's material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

investigations.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
investigations.objective: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
investigations.hypothesis: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the ''Goldilocks'' flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.
investigations.research_impacts: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials' flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)-Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
investigations.objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
investigations.hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
investigations.research_impacts: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
investigations.hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
investigations.objective: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
investigations.hypothesis: Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes, The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
investigations.research_impacts: The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to: 1) More sustainable energy production. 2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions. 3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels). 4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

investigations.title: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
investigations.objective: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
investigations.hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
investigations.research_impacts: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

investigations.title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
investigations.objective: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA's Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
investigations.hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
investigations.research_impacts: Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials. Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

investigations.title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
investigations.objective: By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection. 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames. 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments. 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames. 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
investigations.research_impacts: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

investigations.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
investigations.hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report
investigations.objective: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.
investigations.hypothesis: The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation: In a ug environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at ug conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
investigations.research_impacts: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
investigations.objective: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity. Summarized objectives include: 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
investigations.hypothesis: The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates. The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses: 1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity. 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.
investigations.research_impacts: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

investigations.title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
investigations.hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.
investigations.research_impacts: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.objective: The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 - 2 for extinction limits.
investigations.hypothesis: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
investigations.research_impacts: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE's results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
investigations.objective: In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation was focused on gathering bench mark data to validate the hypothesis of computation models, the details of which are available within the following publications: 1) Smooke, M.D., Hall, R.J., Colket, M.B., Fielding, J., Long, M.B., McEnally, C.S., and Pfefferle, L.D., Investigation of the transition from lightly sooting towards heavily sooting co-flow ethylene diffusion flames. Combustion Theory and Modelling, 2004. 8(3): p. 593-606. https://doi.org/10.1088/1364-7830/8/3/009 2) Luque, J., Jeffries, J.B., Smith, G.P., Crosley, D.R., Walsh, K.T., Long, M.B., and Smooke, M.D., CH(A-X) and OH(A-X) optical emission in an axisymmetric laminar diffusion flame. Combustion and Flame, 2000. 122(1/2): p. 172-175. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-2180(00)00112-7 3) Walsh, K.T., Fielding, J., Smooke, M.D., and Long, M.B., Experimental and computational study of temperature, species, and soot in buoyant and non-buoyant coflow laminar diffusion flames. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 2000. 28: p. 1973-1979. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0082-0784(00)80603-7 4) Walsh, K.T., Long, M.B., Tanoff, M.A., and Smooke, M.D., Experimental and computational study of CH, CH*, and OH* in an axisymmetric laminar diffusion flame. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 1998. 27(Vol. 1): p. 615-623. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0082-0784(98)80453-0
investigations.research_impacts: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
investigations.hypothesis: The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.
investigations.research_impacts: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
investigations.objective: A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damk hler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damk hler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.
investigations.hypothesis: The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. Each description of the flames obtained from the experiment, including measurements of aspects of the flame structure, growth or flame front velocities, and the specific test conditions where steady state flames, flame extinctions, flame front instabilities, soot suppression limits, etc., comprise a rigorous test of the detailed model. Together they provide a measure of the comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic and transport models. The numerical simulation is also being used as a predictive tool to develop the science requirements for this experiment, especially the collection of test conditions and most aspects of the measurement systems. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the flight experiment definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work.
investigations.research_impacts: The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
investigations.hardware: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Reconfiguration of Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
investigations.objective: The primary objectives of this flight experiment are: A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.
investigations.hypothesis: 1. Soot formation requires a region where local C/O ratio and T exceed their critical values, and where strain rate is sufficiently low. 2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K. 3. Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.
investigations.research_impacts: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
investigations.objective: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
investigations.hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
investigations.research_impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world's energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 - 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

investigations.title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.objective: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives were: (1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions. (5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
investigations.hypothesis: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.
investigations.research_impacts: (1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments. (2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions. (3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation (4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

investigations.title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.objective: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. Specific objectives of this investigation were: 1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base. 2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters. 3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability. 4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions. 5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
investigations.hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.
investigations.research_impacts: 1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth. 2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions. 3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety. 4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.

investigations.title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
investigations.objective: This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.
investigations.hypothesis: Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.
investigations.research_impacts: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

source.listed_in: Official Space Apps 2026 'Flame in Freefall' resources tab

notes: Claims are paraphrased. 'quote' is left null on purpose: fill it by string-matching the verbatim sentence from the given PDF page (your 'no quote, no number' rule).
Page numbers are the printed page numbers, which equal the PDF page index in this file.
The guide is from 2015. Anything marked status='planned_2015' describes plans at that time, not results.
psi_accessions map each finding to the PSI investigations it relates to. An empty list means the experiment is not in PSI.

findings.claim: Droplet tests showed the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity, so inert-gas suppressant standards written for Earth do not give the same safety margin in low gravity.
findings.mission_lens_note: Direct evidence that Earth-based suppression standards are not conservative. Fuel is liquid droplets, not habitat solids.

findings.claim: FLEX found a limiting oxygen index for heptane and methanol droplets that is well below the normal-gravity value and below what had been predicted.
findings.mission_lens_note: Checkable against the FLEX experimental table (274 runs, O2 mole fraction 0.12 to 0.34).

findings.claim: After the visible hot flame went out, large alkane droplets kept vaporizing because a low-temperature cool flame was still burning; this was unexpected and initially doubted by the community.
findings.mission_lens_note: A fire that looks extinguished may not be. Relevant to detection and to post-fire procedures.

findings.claim: Reduced gravity favors very weak, persistent flames that are invisible to the eye and can re-ignite on their own long after the visible flame is gone; the conditions for this are poorly understood.
findings.mission_lens_note: Explicitly stated knowledge gap. Good candidate for a 'what we do not know' card.

findings.claim: The safety margin once assumed for microgravity came from quiescent tests and may not hold in real spacecraft, where ventilation flow strengthens flames.
findings.mission_lens_note: Flow speed is a required axis next to O2 and pressure.

findings.claim: At the low flow speeds of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials burn at lower oxygen concentrations than they do in normal gravity.
findings.mission_lens_note: The guide itself names partial gravity. Supports the gravity axis from an official challenge resource.

findings.claim: Materials ignite more easily in low gravity because the fuel surface loses less heat to natural convection.
findings.mission_lens_note: Ignition, not spread. PSI tables carry little ignition data.

findings.claim: In slow airflow a flame can spread upstream, into the incoming air, which is the opposite of what happens in normal gravity.
findings.mission_lens_note: Saffire tables record flow direction (concurrent or opposed) per sample, so this can be shown with PSI rows.

findings.claim: Radiation matters: heat lost by radiation from the surface lowers flammability, while an external radiant heat source makes materials ignite and spread faster.
findings.mission_lens_note: External heat flux is an axis PSI tables do not cover.

findings.claim: BASS ran in the ISS glovebox from March 2012, normally in cabin air, and later used nitrogen to reach oxygen levels as low as 17 percent.
findings.mission_lens_note: Matches the BASS-II table (initial O2 13.6 to 22.2 percent). Explains why PSI solids data sits at or below air.

findings.claim: BASS tests the hypothesis that, given enough ventilation, a material in microgravity burns as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity.
findings.mission_lens_note: Same hypothesis text appears in the PSI-25 metadata. Label as hypothesis, not result.

findings.claim: In microgravity the best place to aim a suppressant is not obvious; depending on geometry the stream can be ineffective or can feed the flame by pulling in oxygen.
findings.mission_lens_note: Earth rule (aim at the base) does not transfer.

findings.claim: Early BASS results showed that nitrogen blown at a flame can make it stronger rather than put it out.
findings.mission_lens_note: Counter-intuitive and memorable. Marked 'early results' in the source.

findings.claim: BASS results indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
findings.mission_lens_note: The single most important finding for the pitch. Stated as a result here, as a suspicion on p.22 to 23 (see RG-15).

findings.claim: Drop-tower results suggest the current Test 1 might not be conservative; a planned investigation would map microgravity flammability against oxygen, flow and pressure to measure the real oxygen margin.
findings.section: Correlation of Flammability between Normal and Microgravity (continues on p.23)
findings.mission_lens_note: Same claim as RG-14 with weaker wording and weaker evidence type. Useful example for certainty grading: two statements, different strength.

findings.claim: Local application of suppressant is not enough to extinguish: the jet entrains air and keeps the flame alive even with cabin airflow switched off.
findings.mission_lens_note: Bears directly on the 'turn off the fans' procedure.

findings.claim: The flammability boundary for solids has a minimum oxygen limit at a gas speed of roughly 10 cm/s, which is also where flame spread is fastest, and that speed is typical of spacecraft ventilation.
findings.mission_lens_note: The worst-case flow is the normal operating flow. BASS-II and Saffire tables carry flow settings (Saffire at 20 to 30 cm/s).

findings.claim: Theory, backed by reduced-gravity aircraft tests, indicates ignition is faster at sub-buoyant airflow and that the critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be about half the normal-gravity value.
findings.section: External Heat Flux Effects on the Ignitability and Suppression of Materials in Microgravity
findings.mission_lens_note: Model-led finding with short test times. Lower certainty than flight results.

findings.claim: As of 2015 there was no test method designed specifically to determine the fire hazard of materials under exploration-atmosphere conditions.
findings.section: External Heat Flux Effects on the Ignitability and Suppression of Materials in Microgravity
findings.mission_lens_note: Explicit gap statement tied to exploration atmospheres. Check whether it still holds before citing as current.

findings.claim: SoFIE was designed for chamber atmospheres of 10 to 40 percent oxygen at 0.2 to 1.5 atm with ventilation-range flows of 0 to 30 cm/s, so it can cover exploration atmospheres.
findings.section: Solid-Fuel Combustion/Material Flammability (flow range on p.21; see also p.38)
findings.mission_lens_note: IMPORTANT: SoFIE is not in PSI. High-oxygen solids data may exist outside PSI. Word the gap as 'not in the public PSI record', never as 'never tested'.

findings.claim: A candle on Mir burned for more than 45 minutes in some tests and kept burning down to a lower ambient oxygen fraction than the same candle would on Earth.
findings.mission_lens_note: Disproves 'a steady flame cannot exist without buoyancy'. Not in PSI.

findings.claim: Flames near their limit in microgravity often oscillate, sometimes for over a minute, before going out; over solids a finger-like smoldering front can appear.
findings.mission_lens_note: Near-limit behavior differs from Earth blow-off.

findings.claim: Three long-held beliefs were shown to be wrong: that a steady fire cannot exist in still microgravity air, that a fire goes out by itself once ventilation stops, and that Earth fire standards are very conservative for space.
findings.evidence_type: program summary citing Friedman and Ross 2001, Ruff et al. 2009
findings.mission_lens_note: Strong framing for the pitch: three myths. Check your deck's ventilation slide against the second one.

findings.claim: Smoke particles from microgravity flames are a very different size, so detectors tuned for Earth smoke would look for the wrong signature.
findings.mission_lens_note: Links to SAME-R table (109 runs: Kapton, Silicone, Lampwick, Pyrell, Teflon).

findings.claim: A detector that watches particulates and chemical species together beat current aircraft smoke detectors on both false-alarm rejection and real-event detection in joint testing with the FAA.
findings.mission_lens_note: Earth-benefit item: aviation safety.

findings.claim: DAFT measured background aerosol levels on the ISS and SAME measured the particle-size distribution of smoke from spacecraft materials, to guide future smoke-detector design.
findings.mission_lens_note: Describes what was measured, not a quantitative finding.

findings.claim: Water-mist portable extinguishers were certified for flight after the STS-107 Mist experiment; the first two of nine went to the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units.
findings.mission_lens_note: Research that changed hardware on orbit. Not in PSI.

findings.claim: The Burning Rate Emulator aims to judge whether existing flammability test methods are relevant for low and partial gravity, using a gas-fed porous burner to imitate solid and liquid fuels.
findings.mission_lens_note: The one ACME experiment aimed at fire prevention. PSI-20 table has 18 rows.

findings.claim: In low gravity the onset of smoke production from jet flames differs substantially from normal gravity and from earlier predictions, and soot particles differ in size and structure.
findings.mission_lens_note: Supports RG-24 from the gas-flame side. SPICE table has 469 rows.

findings.claim: Spacecraft often run at an oxygen fraction above that of air, offer few ways to escape, and tolerate almost no damage to life support, which is why NASA relies on strict material control, design standards and mandatory suppression systems.
findings.mission_lens_note: Context for why oxygen level is the central axis.

facts: Pre-flight pad test, cabin pressurized with 100% oxygen, hatches closed.
Board could not pin the ignition source; found evidence of arcing in wires near the environmental control system.
Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere the fire spread quickly; temperature and pressure rose until the Command Module pressure vessel ruptured.
Crew died of asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases; burns were likely survivable.
Three-piece hatch took 90 s to open under ideal conditions and could not be opened under raised pressure.
Test was rated non-hazardous, so no rescue process was defined.
Changes: unified hatch openable in 3 s; amount and location of combustible material restricted; 3,000-page board report.
Oxygen tank 2 exploded on day three en route to the Moon; it also damaged tank 1.
Loss of fuel cells threatened all power and water; crew used the Lunar Module as a lifeboat.
Oxygen-system hazard, not a cabin fire: use lightly.
Six crew aboard during a handover.
A solid-fuel oxygen generator canister ignited, throwing a roughly three-foot flame with sparks and molten metal.
Flame blocked the path to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles.
Crew put on oxygen masks and used three extinguishers; fire burned several minutes.
Life support took several hours to clear the smoke.
The same generator type had been used more than 2,500 times without incident.
Likely cause after two years of study: latex glove material inside the canister.

earth_benefits.title: Fireman's Air Tanks
facts: Developed with NASA Johnson.
20 lb pack for 30 min of air, 13 lb lighter than conventional tanks, 4,500 psi.
Aluminum liner wrapped in resin-impregnated glass fiber.

earth_benefits.title: Fire Detector
facts: Incipient fire detector first used on the Space Shuttle orbiters.
Tells combustion particles apart from dust, so fewer false alarms.
Sensors can be networked for mines; warns before visible flame and smoke.

earth_benefits.title: Fire Attire (Project FIRES)
facts: NASA with the U.S. Fire Administration, managed by Marshall.
Applies lightweight fire-resistant spacesuit materials to firefighter gear.
Field evaluation with 14 municipal fire departments.

data_insights.claim: BASS-II solids were tested at initial O2 from 13.6% to 22.2% (129 runs).
data_insights.source: PSI-25 BASS-II table, column 'Calibrated initial O2 % by vol'

data_insights.claim: FLEX: 274 runs; O2 mole fraction 0.12 to 0.34; 24 runs at O2 >= 0.30; 0 of those at 380-470 mmHg (window around 8.2 psia = 424 mmHg). Test end: Extinction 186, Disruption 61, Completion 27.
Saffire I-III solids burned at about 21.5-22.1% O2 with 20-30 cm/s flow.
Saffire-II silicone 0.27 mm (sample 2-1): micro-g burn length ~0, while the 1-g reference burned completely. Space is not always worse.

ACME BRE tested the exploration atmosphere: its objective lists 8.2 psia / 34% O2 and 10.2 psia / 26.5%, and its table records 34% and 40% O2 test days. Its burner emulates solid and liquid fuels with gas.
data_insights.important: Corrects the earlier claim that nothing in PSI reaches the exploration atmosphere. Solids and FLEX droplets do not; BRE does.

data_insights.claim: BRE: quasi-steady burning matching materials like PMMA and Nylon continued with no airflow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres, while the same flames at 21% O2 self-extinguished quickly. Turning off ventilation is an established step in fighting spacecraft fires. Results described as preliminary.
No PSI combustion investigation was run in partial gravity (Moon or Mars); all flight data is microgravity, ground studies are models or 1g lab work.

BASS (PSI-26) burned solids from 15.9% to 22.7% O2 at 0.97-1.01 atm. Nitrogen or flow changes are noted as failing (fully or at first) to put the flame out in as-run tests 3, 15, 31, 36, 53, 54, 55, 60, 63, 91 (crew notes).

Earth test vs orbit, same plastic: a cast 1/4-in PMMA rod passes 1g Test 1 only at 14% O2 or less (MOC 14, ULOI 15.7). In BASS-II microgravity, PMMA rods ignited and burned at initial O2 as low as 14.8-15.1% before extinguishing as flow was reduced (Olson O4, O5a, O9), and a rod at 13.6% did not ignite (O12). Link et al. report sustained microgravity spread at 17%. The configurations differ (upward buoyant vs low-speed opposed flow), so show both numbers side by side as different regimes; do not claim one ranks the material above the other.
data_insights.source: G3 Table 7 + PSI-25 BASS-II rows O4, O5a, O9, O12 + G4

data_insights.claim: Smoke in still air is bigger: in SAME-R, unaged diameter of average mass at zero flow is larger than at 8.1 cm/s for every material listed in G2 summary. Larger droplets mean fewer particles for the same mass, which is the SAME hypothesis about detectors missing smoke.

Exposed edges and sample width change Earth-test limits: only PVC showed a significant edge effect (MOC 35 to 39); half-inch samples mostly had lower thresholds than 2.5-in standard samples. Earth limits depend on how the sample is mounted, before gravity even enters.
